name: plink1
why: Whole-genome association toolset is real science you can run, though it is a standard, somewhat dated genetics tool.

brief.what_it_is: PLINK 1.9 is a command-line toolset for whole-genome association analysis of genotype data. It reads PLINK binary (.bed/.bim/.fam) and text (.ped/.map) filesets, plus VCF/BCF, Oxford .gen/.bgen, 23andMe text, and GCTA GRM matrices. It writes new filesets (for example via --make-bed or --recode), summary statistics such as allele frequencies, missingness, Hardy-Weinberg and LD, and association results such as --assoc, --linear, --logistic, and --pca for population structure. The homepage describes it as 'a free, open-source whole genome association analysis toolset, designed to perform a range of basic, large-scale analyses in a computationally efficient manner.'
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a comprehensive update to the original PLINK, written by Shaun Purcell, and developed by Christopher Chang with support from the NIH-NIDDK's Laboratory of Biological Modeling, the Purcell Lab, and others. The point is running standard large-scale genetic association analyses efficiently on genotype datasets.
brief.how_it_works: It is a single 'plink' executable driven by flags, each with a documented role in a pipeline: filter samples and variants, convert or merge filesets, compute statistics, then run tests and post-process reports. The homepage's index covers data management, basic statistics, LD, IBD, population stratification, association, family-based tests, epistasis, and scoring. Development builds are published alongside the stable release, and the changelog lists bug fixes per date.

brief.install_notes: Install with brew install plink1 as the entry point. Prebuilt binaries exist for Linux 64-bit and 32-bit, macOS 64-bit, and Windows 64-bit and 32-bit; the README says Solaris is not explicitly supported but can run the Linux binaries. No runtime or account is needed. The Linux 64-bit binaries need a newer kernel than older releases did: the README says that on a kernel older than about five years you may see 'Kernel too old', and then you must compile from source or use older binaries by replacing the datestamp in the download URL with 20241022. Source and compilation notes are on the developer page.
brief.standout: The page is candid about its own limits. It lists PLINK 1.07 flags it does not support, says its phasing and imputation code is obsolete and points to BEAGLE 3.3, and says the haplotype association commands will return only when phase and dosage input from other programs is supported. It also tells users to keep a permanent copy of the PLINK 1.07 binary if migration is not practical.
brief.status: Maintained as of the page. The stable 1.9.0 release is dated 27 Sep 2026, a development build is dated 5 Oct 2026, and the recent-history changelog runs to 5 Oct 2026. However, the homepage explicitly says 'We recommend migrating away from PLINK 1' and links to a PLINK 2.0 page, so it is a maintained but legacy tool. The scout note calls it dated, and the homepage supports that reading.
brief.caveats: Linux binaries can fail with 'Kernel too old' on older kernels (see install notes). Several PLINK 1.07 flags are unsupported in 1.9.0, including --hap, --proxy-assoc, --cnv-list, --segment, and --compress/--decompress (use gzip or pigz instead). Haplotype phasing and imputation are obsolete. The README says Solaris is no longer explicitly supported. Usage questions go to the plink2-users Google group, not to the author's email. The homepage text was cut off at 40000 characters, so the full changelog and command reference were not read.
quotes: PLINK is a free, open-source whole genome association analysis toolset, designed to perform a range of basic, large-scale analyses in a computationally efficient manner.

We recommend migrating away from PLINK 1 here, but if that's not practical, keep a permanent copy of the PLINK 1.07 binary around and modify the relevant lines of your scripts to explicitly refer to it.
PLINK's haplotype phasing and imputation algorithms are obsolete.
